Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette:
The assault happened on a summer night just over a year ago. Nineteen-year-old Maya was walking home from a friend’s apartment when a motorcycle pulled up beside her. The rider—a man whose face she never clearly saw—shouted something in Arabic, and she caught the sharp smell of alcohol on his breath. He grabbed her, dragged her into an alley, and assaulted her. In the moment she froze, certain she was going to die. Later, replaying it, she kept thinking that somebody else would have known how to fight back, would have stopped it from happening. She was just a new wife, barely out of high school, and now those beliefs about the world being a safe, predictable place were shattered.

In the weeks afterward Maya noticed that certain sounds could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore, as if the past had contaminated the present. A motorcycle passing her apartment building would force her to re‑hear the shouting in her head and re‑smell the alcohol, as though she were right back in the alley. These trigger moments made her feel even more convinced that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her—walking alone, feeling confident, trusting her own judgment. She began listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, and she frequently looked behind her when she left the house. The constant vigilance sometimes itself became a trigger: the creak of a floorboard would mimic the sound of footsteps, throwing her into a flashback where she suddenly felt and acted as if the assault were happening again. And those flashbacks, in turn, ramped up her threat monitoring even further, because after one she was certain the danger was still there.

To manage, Maya developed strict strategies. She avoided the anniversary date of the assault, staying in bed with the curtains drawn. She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh. Because the memory returned so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers’ faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light. She stopped going out after dark altogether—it was easier to stay inside than to scan every shadow. She also avoided paying attention to or looking at her own body, because the sight of her limbs and skin reminded her of being held down, and that memory then made her hypervigilant again. The avoidance itself fed the cycle: by staying home at night she had more time to listen for intruders, which kept her threat system active. By not looking at her body she reinforced the idea that she was damaged, that she could no longer be the person she used to be. And the anniversary date, precisely because she dodged it, became a looming trigger that she was constantly aware of, making that entire week one long, tense preparation.

Her negative appraisals deepened her threat behavior. Because she believed another person would have coped better, she felt inadequate and watched for danger even more carefully—as though her own failure to prevent the assault meant she had to be twice as alert now. The threat monitoring, in turn, strengthened her appraisals: every time she found herself checking behind her, she took it as proof that she was not safe and that the world was still hostile. Meanwhile, the act of avoiding her own body triggered additional negative thoughts: she would catch a glimpse of her reflection and think, *I’m not the same person*, which then made her more vigilant about her surroundings, as if the threat was also internal.

Now Maya rarely leaves the apartment. Her husband works during the day, and she spends hours sitting by the window, listening. She quit her part‑time job because the commute required walking past the alley. She has no energy for the friends she once had. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when a delivery motorcycle backfired outside and she found herself on the floor, screaming, unable to distinguish past from present. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again—that the person she was before the assault is gone for good—but she is equally terrified of continuing like this, a prisoner in her own home. She says she just wants to be able to walk to the grocery store without seeing his face.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that traumatic memory causes or becomes a new trigger; rather, memory leads to threat monitoring, which then becomes a trigger, but the direct causal influence of memory on triggers is missing.

The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies (avoidance) lead to or increase intrusive memories; instead, avoidance is driven by memory or leads to threat and negative appraisals, but not to the memory itself.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that traumatic memory causes or becomes a new trigger; rather, memory leads to threat monitoring, which then becomes a trigger, but the direct causal influence of memory on triggers is missing.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not convey that maladaptive strategies (avoidance) lead to or increase intrusive memories; instead, avoidance is driven by memory or leads to threat and negative appraisals, but not to the memory itself.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
